items.stem: 42 students were asked whether they like Art (A), Biology (B) and Chemistry (C). 4 like all three; 8 like A and B; 7 like A and C; 8 like B and C; 21 like A; 16 like B; 16 like C. (a) Complete a three-set Venn diagram. (b) How many like none? (c) How many like exactly one subject?
items.markingKey: Centre 4, pairwise-only regions 4, 3, 4 (M1 A1); single regions 10, 4, 5 (A1); none = 42 − 34 = 8 (A1); exactly one = 19 (A1).

items.stem: A survey in Lima records whether people exercise weekly (E) by age group. Under 30: E 15, not E 29. 30 and over: E 45, not E 85. (a) Find P(E | under 30) and P(E | 30 and over). (b) Decide, with a reason, whether exercising weekly is independent of age group.
items.answer: (a) 15/44 and 9/26 (b) not independent
items.markingKey: (a) conditional probabilities (M1 A1 A1); (b) compare the conditional probabilities or test P(E ∩ U) = P(E)P(U) (M1); conclusion (R1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "complementary events"?
options: A and A′, with P(A′) = 1 − P(A)
The set ξ (or U) of all elements under consideration
A table showing frequencies for two categorical variables at once
Events where the outcome of one does not change the probability of the other: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
items.answer: A and A′, with P(A′) = 1 − P(A)
items.markingKey: A. "complementary events" is A and A′, with P(A′) = 1 − P(A).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "tree diagram".
items.answer: A branching diagram showing the outcomes of successive events with their probabilities on the branches
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a branching diagram showing the outcomes of successive events with their probabilities on the branches. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.
D. Use the definitions of intersection, union and complement.

items.stem: Explain why the row totals of a two-way table must add to the grand total.
items.answer: Every item belongs to exactly one row, so the rows partition the whole data set.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Every item belongs to exactly one row, so the rows partition the whole data set. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why P(A) + P(A′) = 1.
items.answer: Every outcome is either in A or not in A, and not both, so together they cover the whole sample space.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Every outcome is either in A or not in A, and not both, so together they cover the whole sample space. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how you can test whether two events A and B are independent using probabilities.
items.answer: Check whether P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B); if equal, they are independent.
items.markingKey: Check whether P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B); if equal, they are independent. (R1 R1)

items.stem: Explain why (A ∪ B)′ is the same as A′ ∩ B′, using a Venn diagram.
items.answer: Both describe the region outside both circles: not in A or B is the same as not in A and not in B.
items.markingKey: Both describe the region outside both circles: not in A or B is the same as not in A and not in B. (R1 R1)

items.stem: A test detects a condition 95% of the time. Explain why P(positive | condition) is not the same as P(condition | positive).
items.answer: They condition on different groups; P(condition | positive) also depends on how common the condition is and on false positives.
items.markingKey: They condition on different groups; P(condition | positive) also depends on how common the condition is and on false positives. (R1 R1)

items.stem: Explain whether "rolling an even number" and "rolling a 5" on a fair die are mutually exclusive.
items.answer: Yes: 5 is not even, so they cannot both happen.
items.markingKey: Yes: 5 is not even, so they cannot both happen. (R1 A1)

items.stem: A bag contains 4 red and 7 blue counters. Two are taken at random with replacement. Using a tree diagram, find the probability of both red.
items.markingKey: Correct branch probabilities (same for both draws) (M1 A1); multiply along paths and add as needed (M1); 16/121 (A1).

items.stem: In a group of 41 students, 19 study French (F), 18 study Mandarin (M) and 8 do neither. Draw a Venn diagram and find how many do both.
A two-way table: morning: on time 12, delayed 5; evening: on time 6, delayed 10. Find P(on time | evening).
items.markingKey: Correct numerator and denominator from the table (M1 A1); 3/8 (A1).

items.stem: A Venn diagram shows A only: 7, A and B: 5, B only: 13, neither: 3. A person is chosen at random. Find P(A′).
items.markingKey: Correct region(s) identified: 16 (M1); total 28 (A1); P = 4/7 (A1).

items.stem: A bag contains 3 red and 8 blue counters. Two are taken at random without replacement. Using a tree diagram, find the probability of at least one blue.
items.markingKey: Correct branch probabilities (second draw out of 10) (M1 A1); multiply along paths and add as needed (M1); 52/55 (A1).

items.stem: In a group of 31 students, 17 own a bike (F), 15 own a pet (M) and 4 do neither. Draw a Venn diagram and find how many do both.
A two-way table: morning: on time 31, delayed 27; evening: on time 20, delayed 13. Find P(on time | evening).
items.markingKey: Correct numerator and denominator from the table (M1 A1); 20/33 (A1).

items.stem: At a school in Mumbai, 120 students were surveyed: 35 take the bus (B), 26 cycle on some days (C), and 14 do both. (a) Draw a Venn diagram. (b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen student does neither. (c) Given that a student takes the bus, find the probability that they also cycle. (d) Omar says B and C are mutually exclusive. Is she right?
items.answer: (b) 73/120 (c) 2/5 (d) no – 14 students do both
items.markingKey: Regions 21, 14, 12, 73 (M1 A1); (b) (A1); (c) restricted sample space of 35 (M1 A1); (d) reason (R1).

items.stem: Ingrid takes a penalty kick twice. The probability she scores the first is 0.7. If she scores, the probability she scores the next rises by 0.1; if she misses it falls by 0.2. Find the probability she scores exactly once.
items.markingKey: Tree with correct conditional branches (M1 A1); multiply along paths (M1); add relevant paths (M1); 0.29 (A1).

items.stem: 45 students were asked whether they like Art (A), Biology (B) and Chemistry (C). 4 like all three; 5 like A and B; 9 like A and C; 7 like B and C; 15 like A; 20 like B; 20 like C. (a) Complete a three-set Venn diagram. (b) How many like none? (c) How many like exactly one subject?
items.markingKey: Centre 4, pairwise-only regions 1, 5, 3 (M1 A1); single regions 5, 12, 8 (A1); none = 45 − 38 = 7 (A1); exactly one = 25 (A1).

items.answer: (a) 3/7 and 15/34 (b) not independent
